description_full: Realty Income Corporation, an S&P 500 company, is real estate partner to the world's leading companies. Founded in 1969, they serve their clients as a full-service real estate capital provider. As of June 30, 2026, they have a portfolio of over 15,500 properties in all 50 U.S. states, the U.K., and eight other countries in Europe. They are known as (The Monthly Dividend Company) and have a mission to invest in people and places to deliver dependable monthly dividends that increase over time. Since their founding, they have declared 676 consecutive monthly dividends and are a member of the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats index for having increased dividend for over 31 consecutive years. Realty Income Corporation was founded in 1969 and was incorporated in Maryland.
ceo_bio: Mr. Sumit  Roy | President, CEO & Director | Age 55 | Compensation: $7.1M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 544 people. Revenue per employee of $10.6M ranks in the top quartile among Real Estate peers, with revenue growing 21%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $7.1M of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $57K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (6/10).
financial_summary: Realty Income Corporation is a large-cap real estate business with a $56.1B market cap on $5.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +20% over the past three years and +19% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $3.9B in free cash flow — roughly 67 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.77× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.1× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 39% operating margin runs 16pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.95x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 1.6% of sector revenue and 3.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+11.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 13% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 17% and a beta of 0.45, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $388.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 48% in the 2020 crash, 25% in the 2022 bear market and 48% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 34% below its DCF fair value of $89.02, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 80%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $71.80 to $115 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Real Estate peers: P/E 40.3 vs 23.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 57% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 21 covering analysts target $63.54 on average, 8% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.13).
It converts 67% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.77x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 67%.
ROE of 3% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.21 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 19.8% over 3 years, 28.3% over 5 years and 18.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 28.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 29.1% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.1x depreciation (2.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 82%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.0% (5.6% in dividends, less 4.2% of net share issuance).
The share count has grown 10.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 222% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 544 employees, each generates about $10.6M of revenue, 4.6x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 20.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $7.1M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $7.1M (1x revenue per employee).
